subtopic: Sepsis — risk stratification with qSOFA
vignette: A 79-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her daughter because of fever and a productive cough for 2 days. She has a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. She is alert and answers questions appropriately. Temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F), pulse is 108/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Oxygen saturation is 94% on room air. Crackles are heard at the right lung base. A chest radiograph shows a right lower lobe infiltrate. The patient is being evaluated for possible pneumonia.
leadIn: Which of the following additional findings best identifies this patient as being at increased risk of poor clinical outcomes from this infection?

options.a: Temperature of 39.2°C (102.6°F)
options.c: White blood cell count of 15,000/mm³
options.d: Heart rate of 120/min
options.e: Blood glucose of 190 mg/dL

explanation: In a patient with suspected infection, the **qSOFA score** identifies patients at higher risk of poor outcomes such as prolonged ICU stay or in-hospital mortality. The three criteria are **respiratory rate ≥22/min**, **altered mentation**, and **systolic blood pressure ≤100 mm Hg**; two or more indicate high risk. A respiratory rate of 24/min is one of these criteria, and combined with her age and diabetes it should prompt closer monitoring and consideration of early, aggressive care.

distractorExplanations.a: Fever is part of the SIRS criteria and confirms infection, but it does not predict mortality the way qSOFA variables do.
distractorExplanations.c: Leukocytosis is a SIRS criterion and a marker of inflammation, not a validated predictor of poor outcome in suspected sepsis.
distractorExplanations.d: Tachycardia is a SIRS criterion and is common in many febrile illnesses, but it carries less prognostic weight than the qSOFA variables.
distractorExplanations.e: Hyperglycemia may reflect stress or diabetes but is not a component of any sepsis risk-stratification score.

teachingPoint: qSOFA (respiratory rate ≥22/min, altered mentation, systolic BP ≤100 mm Hg) predicts poor outcomes in suspected infection; SIRS criteria (fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis) identify inflammation but do not stratify mortality risk.
note: qSOFA needs two criteria; the keyed finding gives one, so the stem does not meet the rule its explanation teaches.

subtopic: Post-MI pharmacotherapy and LV dysfunction
vignette: A 59-year-old man is on postoperative day 4 after primary PCI with a drug-eluting stent to the left anterior descending artery for an anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction. He had an uncomplicated hospital course with no chest pain, arrhythmias, or heart failure symptoms, and he is ambulating in the hallway without dyspnea. Medications started on admission include aspirin, ticagrelor, atorvastatin 80 mg daily, and metoprolol succinate. Blood pressure is 132/78 mm Hg, pulse is 64/min, and examination shows no jugular venous distention and clear lungs. Transthoracic echocardiography today shows left ventricular ejection fraction of 34% with anterior wall hypokinesis. Laboratory studies show potassium 4.2 mEq/L and creatinine 0.9 mg/dL.
leadIn: Which of the following should be added to his regimen before discharge?

options.a: Isosorbide mononitrate
options.c: Spironolactone
options.d: Amlodipine
options.e: Lisinopril

explanation: An **ACE inhibitor** is indicated for all patients after myocardial infarction, and its mortality benefit is greatest in those with **left ventricular dysfunction (EF ≤40%)** or heart failure, where it attenuates **adverse ventricular remodeling**. This patient has an infarct-related EF of 34% with preserved renal function and potassium, so starting lisinopril before discharge is guideline-directed therapy; an ARB is substituted for patients who cannot tolerate the cough or angioedema.

distractorExplanations.a: Nitrates relieve angina but do not improve survival after infarction, and this patient has no angina on maximal statin and antiplatelet therapy.
distractorExplanations.b: Digoxin reduces hospitalizations in chronic systolic heart failure but has no mortality benefit and no role in a patient with LV dysfunction but no heart failure symptoms.
distractorExplanations.c: A mineralocorticoid antagonist is added for post-infarction LV dysfunction when EF is ≤40% with heart failure or diabetes — this asymptomatic patient's beta blocker and ACE inhibitor come first, and stacking all three at once before discharge is not the tested standard.
distractorExplanations.d: Amlodipine is an antianginal and antihypertensive agent with no effect on post-infarction remodeling or mortality.

teachingPoint: Post-MI LV dysfunction (EF ≤40%) is an indication for an ACE inhibitor (or ARB) regardless of symptoms — the remodeling benefit drives the survival gain.
reviewerFlag: Spironolactone in post-MI EF<40% requires diabetes or heart failure symptoms per the key trials; framing it as a distractor is guideline-consistent, but the reviewer should verify current ACC/AHA wording. Guideline from memory, unconfirmed.
note: ACE inhibitor post-MI with EF 34%; spironolactone needs HF symptoms or diabetes. Probe objection was a false alarm.

subtopic: Anthracycline cardiotoxicity
vignette: A 58-year-old woman with locally advanced breast cancer is receiving combination chemotherapy. Four months into treatment she develops dyspnea on exertion and bilateral leg swelling. Examination reveals bibasilar crackles, jugular venous distention, and an S3 gallop. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 32%. Her regimen includes cyclophosphamide, an anthracycline antibiotic, and a monoclonal antibody against HER2.
leadIn: Which of the following mechanisms best explains this patient's cardiomyopathy?

options.a: Deposition of immune complexes along the myocardial basement membrane
options.b: Binding of HER2 signaling needed for cardiac myocyte survival
options.c: Acrolein-induced endothelial injury of the myocardial microvasculature
options.d: Coronary vasospasm induced by endothelial dysfunction
options.e: Free radical generation causing oxidative injury to myocyte mitochondria

explanation: The anthracycline antibiotic in her regimen is **doxorubicin**, a well-known cause of dose-dependent, **dil cardiomyopathy** mediated by **free radical generation**. Doxorubicin accumulates in cardiac myocytes, where it cycles through redox reactions that produce reactive oxygen species and overwhelm the heart's limited antioxidant defenses, causing oxidative destruction of myocyte membranes and mitochondria. The result is irreversible myocyte loss and a dilated, poorly contracting ventricle — the basis for the lifetime dose limit used clinically.

distractorExplanations.a: Immune complex deposition along basement membranes characterizes type III hypersensitivity such as post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, not chemotherapy-induced cardiomyopathy.
distractorExplanations.b: Trastuzumab, the HER2 antibody, does cause cardiomyopathy by blocking HER2 cardioprotective signaling, but that toxicity is typically reversible and not free-radical mediated; the question asks for the mechanism of the anthracycline's cardiotoxicity.
distractorExplanations.c: Acrolein, the urotoxic metabolite of cyclophosphamide, causes hemorrhagic cystitis rather than myocardial injury.
distractorExplanations.d: Coronary vasospasm is the cardiotoxic mechanism of 5-fluorouril and, classically, cocaine, neither of which is in this regimen.

teachingPoint: Doxorubicin cardiomyopathy = free radical-mediated myocyte mitochondrial injury; dose-dependent and irreversible.
note: Regimen holds an anthracycline and trastuzumab; either explains the cardiomyopathy.

subtopic: Iron studies interpretation in microcytic anemia
vignette: A 34-year-old woman presents with fatigue and increasing dyspnea on exertion over 3 months. She reports heavy menstrual bleeding since stopping her oral contraceptive 6 months ago. She has no other medical history and takes no medications. On examination she is pale, with a soft flow murmur at the left sternal border; there is no splenomegaly, and there is mild cheilosis at the oral angles. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume 68 fL, and a peripheral smear showing hypochromic, microcytic erythrocytes. Ferritin is 6 ng/mL, serum iron is 25 μg/dL, total iron-binding capacity is 460 μg/dL, and transferrin saturation is 5%.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's anemia?

options.a: Impaired globin chain synthesis
options.b: Inadequate dietary iron availability for erythropoiesis
options.c: Impaired iron incorporation into heme due to lead toxicity
options.d: Sequestration of iron within macrophages despite adequate stores
options.e: Autoimmune destruction of parietal cells

explanation: This patient has **iron deficiency anemia**: microcytic, hypochromic erythrocytes with a **low ferritin**, low serum iron, **high TIBC**, and transferrin saturation well below 15%. Ferritin is the single best first test because it reflects storage iron, and a value this low is essentially diagnostic. Heavy menstrual bleeding is the most common cause of iron deficiency in a premenopausal woman, which fits her timeline after stopping her contraceptive. The correct cause is simply **inadequate iron availability for erythropoiesis** from chronic blood loss.

distractorExplanations.a: Impaired globin chain synthesis describes thalassemia trait, which causes microcytosis but with normal or high ferritin and iron studies.
distractorExplanations.c: Lead toxicity blocks heme synthesis and causes basophilic stippling, but iron studies typically show normal ferritin and normal or elevated iron with a low TIBC.
distractorExplanations.d: Sequestration of iron within macrophages describes anemia of chronic disease, which presents with low iron but also a low TIBC and normal or high ferritin.
distractorExplanations.e: Parietal cell destruction causes B12 deficiency, which is macrocytic, not microcytic.

teachingPoint: Iron deficiency anemia = low ferritin, low serum iron, high TIBC, low transferrin saturation. Anemia of chronic disease = low iron, low TIBC, normal or high ferritin. Thalassemia trait = normal iron studies with disproportionate microcytosis.
note: Keyed "inadequate dietary iron" for menorrhagia; the cause is chronic blood loss.

subtopic: Hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage — Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms
vignette: A 63-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after the sudden onset of left-sided weakness and slurred speech. He has a 15-year history of hypertension, for which he takes medication intermittently. Blood pressure is 210/118 mmHg. Non-contrast head CT shows a hyperdense hemorrhage in the right putamen with extension toward the internal capsule, without subarachnoid blood.
leadIn: Which vascular lesion most likely precipitated this patient's hemorrhage?

options.a: Microaneurysms of the lenticulostriate perforating arteries
options.b: Amyloid deposition in cortical leptomeningeal vessels
options.c: Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms of small penetrating arteries
options.d: Saccular aneurysm at the anterior communicating artery
options.e: Atherosclerotic plaque rupture at the carotid bifurcation

explanation: Chronic hypertension causes **hyaline arteriolosclerosis** of the small penetrating arteries, which then develop **Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms** that rupture. Because the **lenticulostriate arteries** are thin-walled perforators carrying high-pressure flow, hypertensive hemorrhage occurs at classic deep sites: the **putamen** (most common), thalamus, pons, and cerebellum. The acute onset, markedly elevated blood pressure, and hyperdense basal ganglia hemorrhage on non-contrast CT are the recognized pattern.

distractorExplanations.a: This names the correct artery territory but the wrong lesion; the vessel pathology in chronic hypertension is Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysm formation, not a separate microaneurysm type.
distractorExplanations.b: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy causes lobar hemorrhage in normotensive elderly patients, not deep basal ganglia hemorrhage in a hypertensive patient.
distractorExplanations.d: Saccular (berry) aneurysm rupture produces subarachnoid hemorrhage, which is absent on this patient's CT.
distractorExplanations.e: Carotid atherosclerosis leads to thromboembolic ischemic stroke, not a hyperdense hemorrhage on non-contrast CT.

teachingPoint: Hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage: Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms of the lenticulostriate perforators rupture in the putamen, thalamus, pons, and cerebellum.
note: A and C both describe Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms of lenticulostriate perforators.

subtopic: Transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy — distinguishing ATTR from AL and treatment selection
vignette: A 76-year-old man is evaluated for eight months of progressive exertional dyspnea and orthopnea. He describes the sensation of his heart pounding when he lies on his left side. He has bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome dating back ten years, treated surgically, and a remote six-year history of hypertension that resolved without medication changes. Medications are lisinopril and furosemide; the furosemide was recently increased with little improvement in his edema. On examination, blood pressure is 104/62 mm Hg, pulse is 88/min and irregularly irregular. Jugular venous pressure is 11 cm. Lung bases are dull with fine crackles. There is 3+ pretibial edema. ECG shows low-voltage QRS complexes, a first-degree AV block, and atrial fibrillation. Echocardiography shows concentric biventricular wall thickening with a sparkling-appearing myocardium, a preserved ejection fraction, and grade II diastolic dysfunction. Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation show no monoclonal protein, and serum free light-chain ratios are normal. Troponin T is mildly elevated and NT-proBNP is markedly elevated.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic study?

options.a: Cardiac MRI with late gadolinium enhancement
options.b: Endomyocardial biopsy with Congo red staining
options.c: Technetium-99m pyrophosphate scintigraphy
options.d: Serum free light-chain assay in three months
options.e: Coronary CT angiography

explanation: Concentric wall thickening with a **low-voltage ECG** and diastolic dysfunction identifies an **infiltrative cardiomyopathy**, and the long-standing **bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome** points toward amyloid. The negative **serum and urine immunofixation and normal free light-chain ratio** exclude AL amyloidosis, leaving **transthyretin (ATTR) cardiac amyloidosis** as the cause. Because AL has been ruled out serologically, **technetium-99m pyrophosphate scintigraphy** can noninvasively confirm ATTR by demonstrating intense myocardial uptake, sparing this frail patient an endomyocardial biopsy — which is reserved for cases where AL cannot be excluded.

distractorExplanations.a: Cardiac MRI can suggest infiltration with late gadiolinium enhancement, but it cannot distinguish amyloid type or confirm ATTR the way a grade 2 or 3 pyrophosphate uptake pattern does.
distractorExplanations.b: Biopsy is the gold standard, but once AL is excluded serologically, a positive pyrophosphate scan confirms ATTR without the procedural risk in an elderly patient with heart failure.
distractorExplanations.d: The free light-chain studies are already normal; repeating them delays the diagnosis without changing the pretest probability of AL.
distractorExplanations.e: Coronary CT angiography evaluates epicardial coronary disease, which would not explain low voltage, biventricular thickening, and diastolic dysfunction with a preserved ejection fraction.

teachingPoint: Once AL amyloidosis is excluded by normal monoclonal protein studies, technetium-99m pyrophosphate scintigraphy noninvasively confirms transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis; biopsy is reserved for cases where AL remains possible.
reviewerFlag: PYP scintigraphy as the noninvasive standard for ATTR after AL exclusion is well established, but the exact uptake grading terminology (grade 2/3, from memory, unconfirmed) is not tested in the item. Typo check: distractor c contains 'gadiolinium' — flagged for editor correction to 'gadolinium'.
note: PYP scintigraphy after AL excluded.

subtopic: Chest pain risk stratification and disposition
vignette: A 57-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 2 hours of intermittent left-sided chest tightness that began at rest, lasted 10 minutes per episode, and has now resolved completely. She has a 25-pack-year smoking history, hypertension treated with amlodipine, and a sister who had a myocardial infarction at age 60. She is diaphoretic during the episodes but has never had exertional chest pain. Blood pressure is 136/82 mm Hg, pulse is 80/min, and examination is unremarkable. ECG shows normal sinus rhythm with nonspecific T-wave flattening in the lateral leads that is unchanged from a tracing in her chart from 2 years ago. High-sensitivity troponin T is 14 ng/L (reference <22) on arrival and 16 ng/L at 3 hours. She has been pain-free for the past hour.
leadIn: What is the most appropriate disposition for this patient?

options.a: Discharge home with instructions to return if pain recurs
options.b: Discharge home with a 7-day ambulatory ECG monitor
options.c: Immediate invasive coronary angiography
options.d: Admit to a monitored bed for noninvasive ischemia testing
options.e: Admit to the coronary care unit and begin heparin infusion

explanation: Two negative **high-sensitivity troponins** drawn 3 hours apart with an unchanged ECG exclude myocardial infarction, but they do not exclude **underlying obstructive coronary disease**. Her presentation is still an **acute chest pain syndrome with intermediate risk** — rest pain, diaphoresis, smoking, hypertension, and premature family history — so the guideline pathway after rule-out of infarction is **objective ischemia testing**, with a stress test or CT coronary angiography, before she can be safely discharged. Admitting her to a monitored bed for that test balances the small but real risk of missed unstable angina against the cost of an unnecessary catheterization.

distractorExplanations.a: Discharge without testing is reserved for patients who are truly low risk — her rest pain with diaphoresis and risk factor burden leave unstable angina a live possibility despite negative troponins.
distractorExplanations.b: Ambulatory monitoring detects arrhythmia, not obstructive coronary disease; it cannot answer the ischemia question her presentation raises.
distractorExplanations.c: Immediate angiography is indicated for infarction or ongoing refractory ischemia — both excluded here by the troponin trend and her pain-free state.
distractorExplanations.e: Anticoagulation is for ACS with confirmed infarction or clear ongoing ischemia; with infarction ruled out and pain resolved, therapeutic heparin exposes her to bleeding risk without benefit.

teachingPoint: Negative serial high-sensitivity troponins exclude MI, not obstructive CAD — intermediate-risk chest pain still needs ischemia testing before discharge.
reviewerFlag: Exact disposition (monitored bed vs chest-pain unit vs structured observation pathway) varies by institution; the tested principle is ischemia testing before discharge in intermediate-risk patients. Guideline from memory, unconfirmed.
note: Intermediate-risk chest pain after negative hs-troponins: ischemia testing. Disposition wording varies by institution.

subtopic: Adult coarctation of the aorta
vignette: A 27-year-old man is evaluated at a routine insurance physical after a blood pressure reading of 158/96 mm Hg in the right arm. He reports occasional exertional leg fatigue but no chest pain or dyspnea. He takes no medications and has no allergies. His father had coronary disease at age 60. Blood pressure is 156/94 mm Hg in the right arm and 148/92 mm Hg in the left arm, and 102/66 mm Hg in the legs; pulse is 70/min. Examination shows a prominent pulsation in the suprasternal notch and a soft bruit over the left interscapular area. Femoral pulses are reduced and delayed compared with the radial pulses. Transthoracic echocardiography shows a discrete narrowing of the descending thoracic aorta just distal to the left subclavian artery with a peak gradient of 45 mm Hg across the lesion, normal bicuspid valve function, and normal left ventricular systolic function.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.a: Lisinopril therapy with blood pressure reassessment in 3 months
options.b: Amlodipine therapy with blood pressure reassessment in 3 months
options.c: Surgical resection with end-to-end anastomosis
options.d: Percutaneous balloon angioplasty with stent placement
options.e: Metoprolol therapy with exercise stress testing in 6 weeks

explanation: Upper-extremity hypertension with **radio-femoral delay**, a blood pressure gradient between the arms and legs, and an interscapular bruit identify **coarctation of the aorta**, confirmed by echocardiography with a gradient >20 mm Hg. In an adult with a discrete native coarctation and normal left ventricular function, **percutaneous balloon angioplasty with stent placement** is the preferred intervention, relieving the obstruction and lowering blood pressure in one procedure.

distractorExplanations.a: ACE inhibitors lower blood pressure but do not correct the mechanical obstruction, which carries ongoing risk of left ventricular hypertrophy, heart failure, and aneurysm formation.
distractorExplanations.b: Medical antihypertensive therapy alone is inadequate; the gradient of 45 mm Hg meets criteria for intervention.
distractorExplanations.c: Surgical repair is preferred in neonates and infants or in long-segment coarctation; in adults with a discrete lesion, stent angioplasty avoids the morbidity of thoracotomy.
distractorExplanations.e: Beta blockade does not address the obstruction, and stress testing adds nothing to an already confirmed anatomic diagnosis.

teachingPoint: Adult coarctation presents with arm-leg blood pressure discrepancy, radio-femoral delay, and interscapular bruit; a discrete native coarctation with a significant gradient is treated with percutaneous stent angioplasty.
reviewerFlag: Guideline from memory, unconfirmed: threshold gradient (>20 mm Hg) for coarctation intervention and preference for stent angioplasty over surgery in adults with discrete native coarctation.
note: Adult discrete coarctation: stent angioplasty.

subtopic: Nephrotic syndrome — infection risk and prevention
vignette: A 7-year-old girl is seen for routine follow-up of minimal change disease diagnosed 14 months ago. She has had two relapses, each treated successfully with oral prednisone, and is currently in remission off all medications. Her father asks how future infections can be prevented, because her cousin with the same condition was hospitalized last year with a serious abdominal infection. She is fully immunized for her age and has no allergies. Examination is unremarkable today, with no edema and a normal blood pressure.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate preventive measure for this patient?

options.a: Daily penicillin prophylaxis for 2 years
options.c: Abdominal ultrasound every 6 months
options.d: Annual influenza vaccination only
options.e: Monthly intravenous immunoglobulin infusions

explanation: Children with nephrotic syndrome are at increased risk of **encapsulated organism infections**, especially **pneumococcal peritonitis and sepsis**, because urinary loss of **immunoglobulin G and complement** impairs opsonization. The recommended preventive measures are pneumococcal vaccination and annual influenza vaccination; influenza infection is a common trigger of relapse, so preventing it has a dual benefit. Additional immunoglobulin levels are not routinely needed, and prophylactic antibiotics are not standard for a child in remission.

distractorExplanations.a: Continuous antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended for nephrotic syndrome in remission; it promotes resistance and is reserved for specific indications such as recurrent UTI with reflux.
distractorExplanations.c: Surveillance abdominal ultrasound does not prevent infection; it has no role in the routine monitoring of minimal change disease.
distractorExplanations.d: Influenza vaccination alone is insufficient — the highest-morbidity infection in nephrotic children is pneumococcal, and pneumococcal vaccination is a core part of the preventive strategy.
distractorExplanations.e: Immunoglobulin infusions are used only for patients with documented hypogammaglobulinemia and serious recurrent infections, not as routine prophylaxis.

teachingPoint: Nephrotic syndrome causes urinary loss of IgG and complement, predisposing to pneumococcal peritonitis and sepsis; pneumococcal and annual influenza vaccination are the key preventive measures.
reviewerFlag: Vaccination schedule details for children with nephrotic syndrome are from memory, unconfirmed; the core recommendation (pneumococcal plus influenza vaccination) is well established in pediatric nephrology guidance.
note: Pneumococcal plus annual influenza vaccination in nephrotic syndrome.

subtopic: Hepatitis A — post-exposure prophylaxis
vignette: A 26-year-old woman calls the clinic 3 days after her roommate was diagnosed with acute hepatitis A. The roommate developed jaundice and was confirmed by IgM anti-HAV testing. The two share a bathroom and kitchen, and the patient helped care for her during the past week. The patient is healthy, has never had hepatitis A, and does not know whether she has been vaccinated. She takes no medications and has no chronic medical conditions. She has no jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, or fever today. Her immunization records cannot be located.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate management of this patient?

options.a: Hepatitis A vaccine and immune globulin
options.c: Hepatitis A vaccine alone
options.d: Hepatitis A IgM antibody testing today
options.e: No prophylaxis; advise hand hygiene and return if symptomatic

explanation: This patient has a **household exposure to confirmed hepatitis A** within the past 2 weeks, the window in which **post-exposure prophylaxis** is effective. For healthy people aged 1 through 40 years, the recommended prophylaxis is the **hepatitis A vaccine alone**; immune globulin is added only for infants under 1 year, adults over 40, and patients who are **immunocompromised or have chronic liver disease**, because vaccine responses may be blunted in those groups. This patient is 26 and healthy, so vaccine alone is appropriate and also confers durable immunity against future exposures.

distractorExplanations.a: Combining vaccine with immune globulin is reserved for patients over 40, the immunocompromised, or those with chronic liver disease; in a healthy 26-year-old it unnecessarily reduces vaccine immunogenicity.
distractorExplanations.b: Immune globulin alone provides only temporary passive protection and is used when the patient cannot receive vaccine or is in a group with poor vaccine response.
distractorExplanations.d: IgM testing would only detect established infection; it does not address the need to prevent infection after a recent exposure.
distractorExplanations.e: Doing nothing forfeits the effective 2-week window for post-exposure prophylaxis in a clearly exposed household contact.

teachingPoint: After hepatitis A exposure, healthy people aged 1–40 receive the hepatitis A vaccine alone; add immune globulin for age >40, immunocompromise, or chronic liver disease — all within 2 weeks.
reviewerFlag: Guideline from memory, unconfirmed: ACIP age cutoff of 40 years for vaccine-only post-exposure prophylaxis should be verified.
note: Healthy 26-year-old: hepatitis A vaccine alone as PEP (ACIP).

subtopic: Post-MI ventricular arrhythmia and ICD indication
vignette: A 59-year-old man is recovering in the coronary care unit on hospital day 2 after an anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction, treated with primary angioplasty and stenting of a proximal left anterior descending occlusion. He has been free of chest pain since reperfusion. This morning, telemetry captures a 30-second run of monomorphic ventricular tachycardia at 160/min; his blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg and he is asymptomatic, and the rhythm terminates spontaneously. He is already receiving aspirin, ticagrelor, metoprolol, lisinopril, and atorvastatin. An echocardiogram obtained this morning shows an ejection fraction of 28% with anterior akinesis. Serum potassium is 4.0 mEq/L and magnesium is 2.0 mg/dL; troponin is falling appropriately.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate management of this patient's arrhythmia?

options.a: Reassessment of ejection fraction at least 40 days after the infarct
options.c: Amiodarone loading followed by lifelong oral therapy
options.d: Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator placement before discharge
options.e: Lidocaine infusion for 48 hours

explanation: Ventricular tachycardia within the first 48 hours after an acute infarct reflects the **electrical instability of the acutely injured myocardium** and does not by itself establish an ICD indication. The decision that matters is what happens once the myocardium has had time to recover: guidelines require **reassessment of ejection fraction at least 40 days post-MI on optimal medical therapy**, because **stunned myocardium** frequently recovers function, and an ICD implanted too early exposes patients to device complications without benefit. If the EF remains ≤35% at that reassessment, primary-prevention ICD implantation is indicated. His hemodynamically tolerated, self-terminating run needs continued beta blockade and electrolyte vigilance, not an acute intervention.

distractorExplanations.b: Electrophysiology study with ablation is reserved for recurrent sustained VT unresponsive to therapy or specific substrates; a single self-terminating run on day 2 does not warrant this.
distractorExplanations.c: Lifelong amiodarone does not improve mortality in this setting and adds pulmonary, thyroid, and hepatic toxicity; beta blockade is the antiarrhythmic backbone after MI.
distractorExplanations.d: ICD implantation within 40 days of an MI is not indicated even with a low ejection fraction, because recovery of stunned myocardium may eliminate the need and early devices carry harm without proven benefit.
distractorExplanations.e: Prophylactic lidocaine was abandoned decades ago because it increased mortality from asystole despite suppressing ventricular ectopy.

teachingPoint: VT within 48 hours of acute MI is treated acutely but does not mandate an ICD. Reassess EF at ≥40 days post-MI on optimal medical therapy; implant an ICD for primary prevention only if EF remains ≤35%.
reviewerFlag: The 40-day post-MI ICD waiting period and EF ≤35% threshold are established guideline values from memory; reviewer should confirm currency.
note: VT within 48 h of MI: reassess EF at 40 days before ICD.

subtopic: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy — sudden death risk stratification and ICD indication
vignette: A 19-year-old collegiate rower is evaluated after an episode of loss of consciousness. He was completing an intense interval session when he felt lightheaded and collapsed; he woke within seconds on the dock without confusion or incontinence. He reports two similar episodes of near-syncope during hard training over the past four months, and occasional exertional chest tightness that resolves with rest. His father died unexpectedly at age 38 while playing basketball; an autopsy was never performed. On examination, vital signs are normal. Cardiac examination reveals a harsh systolic murmur at the left sternal border that intensifies when the patient performs a Valsalva maneuver and softens with passive leg elevation. The carotid upstrokes are brisk. An ECG shows deep T-wave inversions in the lateral precordial leads and prominent septal Q waves. Echocardiography reports asymmetric septal hypertrophy with a resting left ventricular outflow tract gradient of 25 mm Hg and normal systolic function.
leadIn: In addition to activity restriction, which of the following is the most appropriate management for this patient?

options.a: Holter monitoring in three months
options.c: Septal myectomy without device therapy
options.d: Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator placement
options.e: Alcohol septal ablation without device therapy

explanation: Exertional syncope in a young athlete with a **murmur that intensifies with Valsalva** and asymmetric septal hypertrophy establishes **hypertrophic cardiomyopathy** with dynamic outflow tract obstruction. The decision this patient forces is sudden-death prevention, and he carries two major risk factors: **unexplained syncope during exertion** and a **family history of sudden cardiac death** before age 50. Because these risk factors place him at high enough risk for ventricular arrhythmia, the guideline-supported intervention is **implantable cardioverter-defibrillator placement** as primary prevention. Medication and septal reduction therapy address the gradient and symptoms, but they do not protect against the arrhythmic event that killed his father.

distractorExplanations.a: Delaying risk management for surveillance would leave a high-risk patient unprotected; his risk factors justify device therapy now, not further observation.
distractorExplanations.b: Amiodarone suppresses atrial and ventricular ectopy, but it has never been shown to prevent sudden death in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and is not a substitute for device therapy in a high-risk patient.
distractorExplanations.c: Septal myectomy relieves outflow obstruction and symptoms but does not reduce the risk of ventricular fibrillation, which is the threat signaled by his syncope and family history.
distractorExplanations.e: Alcohol septal ablation reduces the gradient but creates scar that can itself be arrhythmogenic, and like myectomy it does not address his sudden-death risk.

teachingPoint: In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, exertional syncope plus a family history of sudden cardiac death are major sudden-death risk factors; the intervention that addresses that risk is an ICD, not gradient-reducing therapy.
reviewerFlag: ICD indication for HCM is based on an individualized risk score; exertional syncope and family history of SCD are established major risk factors driving device decisions in most guidelines. From memory, unconfirmed whether current ESC/ACC wording would mandate ICD for exactly two risk factors versus recommend it — flagged for reviewer.
note: HCM with exertional syncope and family SCD: ICD.

subtopic: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy — sudden death prevention
vignette: A 24-year-old man is evaluated in cardiology clinic after an episode of syncope during a competitive basketball game. He lost consciousness for roughly 20 seconds while sprinting and awoke with confusion that cleared within a minute. He has had exertional dyspnea for the past year but no chest pain. His father died suddenly at age 34 while swimming; an autopsy was never performed. He takes no medications and does not smoke. Blood pressure is 124/72 mmHg and pulse is 62/min. Cardiac examination reveals a harsh systolic ejection murmur at the left sternal border that increases with standing and decreases with squatting; the remainder of the examination is normal. ECG shows deep T-wave inversions in the lateral precordial leads. Echocardiography demonstrates asymmetric septal hypertrophy with a maximal wall thickness of 20 mm, systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve, and a resting left ventricular outflow tract gradient of 60 mmHg; ejection fraction is 68%. He is started on a beta blocker and counseled to avoid competitive athletics.
leadIn: In addition to the beta blocker and activity restriction, which of the following is the most appropriate next step to reduce this patient's risk of death?

options.a: Subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator implantation
options.c: Permanent pacemaker implantation for syncope prevention
options.d: Septal myectomy to relieve the outflow tract gradient
options.e: Amiodarone therapy for ventricular arrhythmia suppression

explanation: This patient has obstructive **hypertrophic cardiomyopathy**, and his syncope on exertion plus a **family history of sudden cardiac death** place him at high risk for **sudden cardiac death** from ventricular arrhythmia. The intervention shown to reduce mortality in high-risk HCM patients is an **implantable cardioverter-defibrillator**, which terminates the ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation that causes these events. Beta blockers and activity restriction address symptoms and exposure, but they do not protect against an arrhythmic arrest; the defibrillator does. Septal reduction is reserved for patients with refractory symptoms despite maximally tolerated medical therapy, and this patient has only New York Heart Association class II symptoms at first presentation.

distractorExplanations.b: Transplantation is considered only for end-stage HCM with refractory heart failure or intractable arrhythmias despite maximal therapy, not at first presentation with preserved systolic function.
distractorExplanations.c: Pacing does not prevent sudden arrhythmic death; it is indicated for conduction disease or bradyarrhythmias, neither of which this patient has.
distractorExplanations.d: Septal myectomy or alcohol ablation improves symptoms and gradient in patients refractory to medical therapy, but gradient reduction has not been established to reduce sudden death risk the way defibrillator implantation has.
distractorExplanations.e: Amiodarone can reduce arrhythmia burden but has not been shown to reduce sudden death risk in HCM and carries substantial long-term toxicity; it does not substitute for defibrillator protection.

teachingPoint: HCM + exertional syncope or family history of sudden death = high sudden-death risk → implantable cardioverter-defibrillator, regardless of symptom therapy.
reviewerFlag: From memory, unconfirmed: ICD indication in HCM based on major risk factors (syncope, family history of sudden death, wall thickness ≥30 mm) — current ESC/ACC-AHA guidance supports defibrillator implantation for patients judged at high risk; exact risk-factor weighting should be verified against the current guideline.
note: HCM high SCD risk: S-ICD reasonable.

subtopic: Complicated parapneumonic effusion requiring drainage
vignette: A 57-year-old man is admitted with cough, fever, and pleuritic left-sided chest pain. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus and drinks 4 cans of beer daily. His temperature is 38.9°C (102°F), pulse is 110/min, respiratory rate is 24/min, blood pressure is 128/74 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation is 93% on room air. Examination reveals crackles and decreased breath sounds over the left lower lung field with dullness to percussion. Chest radiograph shows a left lower lobe infiltrate with a moderate left pleural effusion. He is started on intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin. On hospital day 3, his temperature remains 38.6°C (101.5°F), he continues to have pleuritic pain, and repeat radiograph shows the effusion has increased in size. Diagnostic thoracentesis is performed and shows turbid fluid with a pH of 7.18, glucose of 38 mg/dL, LDH of 3200 U/L, and 6200 neutrophils/µL; Gram stain and culture show no organisms. Lateral decubitus radiograph shows layering without clear loculation.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.a: Continue intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin without drainage
options.b: Insert a chest tube for pleural drainage while continuing intravenous antibiotics
options.c: Repeat therapeutic thoracentesis every 48 hours while continuing antibiotics
options.d: Switch to intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam for broader anaerobic coverage
options.e: Refer for thoracotomy with decortication

explanation: Failure of a patient with pneumonia to defervesce after 48–72 hours of appropriate antibiotics should prompt evaluation for a **parapneumonic effusion**, and this one is biochemically complicated: a **pleural fluid pH <7.20**, glucose <60 mg/dL, and LDH above 1000 U/L mark an effusion that will organize and progress to empyema if left undrained, even when the Gram stain is negative. Because the effusion is free-flowing on the decubitus film, it can be drained by **tube thoracostomy**, which must be combined with continued intravenous antibiotics — drainage alone and antibiotics alone are both insufficient. A negative Gram stain does not downgrade the effusion, as bacteria are frequently cleared from the pleural space while the inflammatory cascade persists. Decortication is reserved for a mature, organized empyema or an effusion that fails to drain after tube placement and fibrinolytics.

distractorExplanations.a: This stops at recognizing that antibiotics were appropriate for pneumonia; a complicated effusion is a closed-space infection that antibiotics cannot penetrate and sterilize on their own.
distractorExplanations.c: Serial thoracentesis is inadequate because the fluid reaccumulates rapidly and the pleural space is not continuously evacuated; intermittent drainage also risks pleural symphysis and trapped lung.
distractorExplanations.d: The issue is not inadequate pathogen coverage but an undrained infected pleural collection; broadening antibiotics without drainage leaves the effusion to organize.
distractorExplanations.e: Decortication is the salvage operation for a thickened, organized fibrous peel after failed tube drainage, not the first intervention for a free-flowing complicated effusion.

teachingPoint: A parapneumonic effusion with pH <7.20, glucose <60, or positive Gram stain/culture requires prompt tube drainage in addition to antibiotics — antibiotics alone are not enough.
reviewerFlag: Thresholds (pH <7.20, glucose <60, LDH >1000) are standard ACCP/First Aid teaching; drainage thresholds are consistent across major guidelines.
note: Complicated parapneumonic effusion: chest tube plus antibiotics.

subtopic: Insulinoma — next step after biochemical confirmation
vignette: A 41-year-old woman is admitted for a supervised 72-hour fast after recurrent episodes of confusion and sweating that occur late in the morning and improve with eating. She has no diabetes and takes no medications. During the fast, at hour 20 her glucose falls to 42 mg/dL and she becomes diaphoretic and tremulous. Laboratory values at that time show insulin 24 microIU/mL (elevated for the glucose level), C-peptide elevated, proinsulin elevated, beta-hydroxybutyrate low, and a sulfonylurea screen negative. Her exam is notable only for a BMI of 31 kg/m2. The fast is terminated and she recovers with intravenous dextrose.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.a: Continue the fast for the full 72 hours before further testing
options.b: Begin empiric diazoxide and reassess symptoms in three months
options.c: Obtain CT or MRI of the abdomen with endoscopic ultrasound for tumor localization
options.d: Repeat the insulin and C-peptide measurements during a second supervised fast
options.e: Measure serum cortisol and growth hormone to assess counter-regulatory failure

explanation: The supervised fast was terminated when she developed **Whipple triad** with inappropriately elevated insulin, C-peptide, and proinsulin, a suppressed **beta-hydroxybutyrate**, and a negative sulfonylurea screen — this is the biochemical signature of **endogenous hyperinsulinism**, i.e. an insulinoma. The diagnosis is now established; repeating the fasting study adds nothing. The next step is **localization**, because these tumors are often small and may be multiple within the MEN1 syndrome: cross-sectional imaging with CT or MRI of the abdomen, frequently complemented by **endoscopic ultrasound**, which is the most sensitive test for small pancreatic lesions.

distractorExplanations.a: The fast ends as soon as Whipple triad is documented with the biochemical panel; continuing it only prolongs dangerous hypoglycemia.
distractorExplanations.b: Diazoxide can suppress insulin secretion, but it is used when surgery is not possible or while awaiting definitive treatment, not as empiric therapy before the tumor is localized.
distractorExplanations.d: The diagnosis is already biochemically confirmed; repeating the fast would expose her to further hypoglycemia without new information.
distractorExplanations.e: Counter-regulatory hormone deficiency causes hypoglycemia with appropriately suppressed insulin; her elevated insulin and C-peptide exclude this, so cortisol and GH testing are not indicated.

teachingPoint: Hypoglycemia with high insulin, C-peptide, and proinsulin plus a negative sulfonylurea screen confirms insulinoma; the next step is tumor localization (CT/MRI, endoscopic ultrasound), not further fasting studies.
reviewerFlag: Endoscopic ultrasound as the preferred localization modality alongside CT/MRI is standard teaching; from memory, unconfirmed against current ENETS guideline specifics.
note: Insulinoma confirmed: localize with CT/MRI plus EUS.

subtopic: Posterior shoulder dislocation evaluation
vignette: A 52-year-old man is evaluated in the emergency department 12 hours after a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. He complains of severe pain in both shoulders and is unable to actively raise either arm away from his side. He holds both arms splinted against his chest in adduction and internal rotation. Vital signs are within normal limits. Passive external rotation of either shoulder is sharply limited by pain and feels mechanically blocked. Standard anteroposterior radiographs of both shoulders are reported as showing no fracture and no definite dislocation, with the humeral heads appearing to sit normally over the glenoids. He has no prior history of shoulder injury or inflammatory arthritis. Neurovascular examination of both upper extremities is intact.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic study to confirm the suspected injury?

options.a: Axillary lateral radiographs of both shoulders
options.b: MRI of both shoulders without contrast
options.c: CT angiography of both shoulder girdles
options.d: Repeat anteroposterior radiographs in external rotation
options.e: Bedside shoulder ultrasonography of both joints

explanation: Generalized seizures produce violent **internal rotation and adduction** of the shoulder, a mechanism that classically causes **posterior shoulder dislocation**, often bilaterally. Posterior dislocations are easily missed on a single **AP radiograph** because the humeral head overlaps the glenoid in that plane and may appear normally located. The finding that the patient is **locked in internal rotation** and blocked on passive external rotation strongly suggests a posterior dislocation that the AP film failed to capture. An **axillary lateral view** visualizes the joint in the axial plane and directly demonstrates posterior displacement of the humeral head relative to the glenoid, making it the most appropriate next study.

distractorExplanations.b: MRI is useful for evaluating associated soft-tissue or labral injury but is not the first study to confirm a suspected posterior dislocation when standard radiography is equivocal.
distractorExplanations.c: CT angiography is indicated when a dislocation is associated with suspected vascular injury, but this patient's neurovascular examination is intact and the priority is to confirm the dislocation itself.
distractorExplanations.d: A repeat AP film, even in external rotation, does not reliably visualize posterior displacement in the axial plane and would not solve the diagnostic problem posed by the initial AP view.
distractorExplanations.e: Shoulder ultrasonography can detect some dislocations but is operator-dependent and does not provide the standardized osseous visualization needed to confirm posterior displacement and guide reduction.

teachingPoint: Posterior shoulder dislocation is a classic complication of seizure or electrocution and is frequently missed on standard AP radiographs. An axillary lateral or scapular Y view is required to confirm the diagnosis. A patient locked in internal rotation after a seizure should be assumed to have a posterior dislocation until proven otherwise.
note: Posterior dislocation after seizure: axillary lateral view.

subtopic: Stroke syndromes — lateral medullary infarct and vertebral artery imaging
vignette: A 49-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 50 minutes after the acute onset of dizziness, slurred speech, and difficulty swallowing. He was lifting a heavy box overhead when he felt a sudden, sharp pain at the base of his neck on the right side, followed within a minute by vertigo and nausea. He has hypertension and hyperlipidemia. His medications are amlodipine and atorvastatin. On examination, blood pressure is 156/94 mm Hg, pulse is 78/min and regular, and respiratory rate is 16/min. He is alert with dysarthric speech. The right pupil is 2 mm and the left is 4 mm in room light; both react briskly. There is mild right ptosis. Pinprick sensation is reduced on the right side of the face and on the left arm and leg. The right palatal curtain fails to elevate on phonation. The right finger-to-nose test is markedly ataxic. Strength, deep tendon reflexes, and plantar responses are normal. Finger-stick glucose is 132 mg/dL. ECG shows normal sinus rhythm.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic study?

options.a: CT angiography of the head
options.c: Carotid duplex ultrasonography
options.d: CT angiography of the head and neck
options.e: MRI of the brain without contrast

explanation: The combination of **ipsilateral Horner syndrome**, **ipsilateral facial** and **contralateral body sensory loss**, dysphagia, and ipsilateral ataxia constitutes the **lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome**, indicating infarction in the territory of the **posterior inferior cerebellar artery**. The PICA arises from the vertebral artery, so the vascular lesion lies in the **vertebrobasilar circulation**. The sudden posterior cervical pain during overhead lifting points to **vertebral artery dissection**, which typically originates in the cervical segment and propagates intracranially. **CT angiography of the head and neck** is required to identify the dissection flap, pseudoaneurysm, or occlusion in the cervical vertebral artery and to assess the intracranial vasculature for thrombectomy candidacy.

distractorExplanations.a: CT angiography of the head alone would miss a cervical vertebral artery dissection, the likely source of this patient's PICA territory infarct.
distractorExplanations.b: Transthoracic echocardiography would pursue a cardioembolic source, but the normal ECG, regular rhythm, and posterior neck pain during mechanical stress favour an arterial dissection.
distractorExplanations.c: Carotid duplex ultrasonography primarily evaluates the anterior circulation and does not reliably assess the vertebral arteries in the neck.
distractorExplanations.e: MRI of the brain could confirm a lateral medullary infarct, but it is slower than CTA and does not identify the cervical vascular lesion driving the acute management decision.

teachingPoint: Lateral medullary infarction localises the lesion to PICA, a vertebral artery branch. When the presentation includes sudden posterior neck pain with mechanical trigger, image the head and neck vasculature with CTA to evaluate for vertebral artery dissection.
note: Lateral medullary syndrome with neck pain: CTA head and neck.

subtopic: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction — diagnosis and first-line therapy
vignette: A 76-year-old woman with a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus is evaluated in the clinic for three months of progressive exertional dyspnea and orthopnea. She reports dyspnea after walking half a block and uses three pillows at night. She currently takes chlorthalidone 25 mg daily and metformin 1000 mg twice daily. On examination, the blood pressure is 158/94 mm Hg, heart rate 82/min, and respiratory rate 20/min. The jugular venous pressure is estimated at 9 cm. Bibasilar crackles are present. There is 1+ pitting edema at the ankles bilaterally. Laboratory studies show a serum sodium of 138 mEq/L, potassium 4.0 mEq/L, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, and BNP 420 pg/mL. An ECG shows normal sinus rhythm with left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage criteria and no ST-T abnormalities. An echocardiogram shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 60%, left atrial volume index of 38 mL/m², and grade 2 diastolic dysfunction with an E/A ratio of 0.7 and deceleration time of 240 ms. The left ventricular wall thickness is 13 mm. There are no regional wall motion abnormalities.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in this patient's management?

options.a: Add carvedilol 3.125 mg orally twice daily
options.c: Add spironolactone 12.5 mg orally daily
options.d: Add amlodipine 5 mg orally daily
options.e: Add ivabradine 5 mg orally twice daily

explanation: This patient meets the criteria for **heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF)**: symptoms and signs of heart failure (exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, crackles, edema, elevated **BNP**), an **LVEF ≥50%**, and objective evidence of diastolic dysfunction with **left atrial enlargement** and a **grade 2 diastolic dysfunction** pattern on echocardiography. In HFpEF, the most critical management step is aggressive **blood pressure control**, as hypertension is the primary driver of the diastolic filling abnormality. The patient remains significantly hypertensive at 158/94 mm Hg despite chlorthalidone. Adding an **ACE inhibitor** provides RAAS blockade to lower blood pressure to target and is the appropriate next antihypertensive agent in a diabetic patient with HFpEF.

distractorExplanations.a: Beta-blockers can reduce heart rate and improve filling time in HFpEF, but they are not first-line for HFpEF management; blood pressure control with RAAS blockade is prioritized, especially when the heart rate is already 82/min and not a limiting factor.
distractorExplanations.c: Spironolactone has shown modest benefit in selected HFpEF populations but is not the first-line agent to add; the immediate priority is achieving blood pressure target with a RAAS inhibitor, and the patient's potassium and renal function are favorable for an ACE inhibitor first.
distractorExplanations.d: Amlodipine is safe and effective for hypertension in HFpEF, but in a diabetic patient, an ACE inhibitor is preferred as the next agent because it provides renal protection and addresses the RAAS activation driving both the hypertension and diastolic dysfunction.
distractorExplanations.e: Ivabradine is indicated for symptomatic HFrEF with a heart rate ≥70 bpm on maximally tolerated beta-blocker therapy; it has no role in HFpEF, where the ejection fraction is preserved and the heart rate is not the primary problem.

teachingPoint: HFpEF is diagnosed by symptoms of heart failure with LVEF ≥50% plus objective evidence of diastolic dysfunction (elevated BNP, left atrial enlargement, abnormal diastolic filling pattern on echocardiography). The cornerstone of management is aggressive blood pressure control, and ACE inhibitors or ARBs are preferred first-line agents, particularly in patients with hypertension, diabetes, or CKD.
note: E/A 0.7 with DT 240 ms is grade 1, labelled grade 2; current first choice (SGLT2i) not offered, key acceptable among options.

subtopic: Diverticular hemorrhage — angiographic localization and embolization after failed endoscopic control
vignette: A 68-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with two episodes of large-volume maroon-coloured stool followed by hematochezia. Her past medical history is notable for diverticulosis, hypertension, and osteoarthritis. Her blood pressure is 104/62 mmHg and her heart rate is 112/min. She is given 1.5 litres of crystalloid and 1 unit of packed red blood cells, and her blood pressure stabilises at 118/72 mmHg. Her hemoglobin is 7.8 g/dL. Colonoscopy is performed within 6 hours and reveals active arterial spurting from a diverticulum in the sigmoid colon. Epinephrine is injected and two hemoclips are placed, but 30 minutes later she passes fresh blood per rectum and her blood pressure drops to 96/58 mmHg. Repeat endoscopic view shows persistent oozing at the clip site.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.a: Segmental colectomy via laparotomy
options.b: Technetium-99m tagged red blood cell scintigraphy
options.c: Mesenteric angiography with selective embolization
options.d: Capsule endoscopy
options.e: Octreotide infusion and observation

explanation: This patient has a **diverticular hemorrhage** that was localized by colonoscopy but could not be controlled endoscopically, as evidenced by recurrent bleeding despite epinephrine injection and hemoclips. After failed endoscopic therapy in a patient who has been resuscitated and stabilized, **mesenteric angiography with selective embolization** is the standard next step. Angiography can both localize the bleeding vessel and deliver superselective coil or particle embolization, with a high success rate and lower morbidity than emergent surgery. Surgery is reserved for patients in whom angiographic embolization fails or who are too unstable to tolerate it.

distractorExplanations.a: Segmental colectomy is the salvage therapy for lower GI bleeding when both endoscopic and angiographic control have failed, or when the patient is too unstable for angiography; it carries significant morbidity in an elderly patient.
distractorExplanations.b: Tagged RBC scintigraphy is a localization tool used when the bleeding source is unknown and the patient is stable; here the source has already been identified by colonoscopy, and the problem is control, not localization.
distractorExplanations.d: Capsule endoscopy is for obscure bleeding in stable patients and provides no therapeutic capability.
distractorExplanations.e: Octreotide is used in variceal bleeding from portal hypertension, not in diverticular arterial hemorrhage, and observation alone is unsafe with ongoing active bleeding.

teachingPoint: The algorithm for diverticular bleeding: resuscitate, then colonoscopy. If endoscopic therapy fails to achieve durable hemostasis, proceed to **mesenteric angiography with selective embolization**. Surgery is the last resort after both endoscopic and angiographic approaches fail.
note: Diverticular bleed after failed endoscopic therapy: angiographic embolization.

subtopic: Aortic Stenosis — Referred for Valve Replacement
vignette: A 76-year-old man is evaluated for 6 months of progressive shortness of breath when climbing stairs and two episodes of near-syncope while walking uphill. He has also had exertional chest pressure relieved by rest over the same period. Past history includes hypertension treated with amlodipine. He has smoked half a pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years. On examination, BP is 145/85 mm Hg and pulse is 78/min and regular. Cardiac auscultation reveals a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to both carotid arteries, with a soft second heart sound. Carotid pulses are delayed in onset and low in amplitude. An echocardiogram shows a calcified, immobile aortic valve with a peak velocity of 4.5 m/s, a mean gradient of 45 mm Hg, and a valve area of 0.7 cm2. Left ventricular systolic function is normal.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.a: Increase the amlodipine dose and reassess symptoms in 3 months
options.c: Repeat echocardiography in 6 to 12 months
options.d: Refer for percutaneous balloon aortic valvuloplasty
options.e: Refer for aortic valve replacement

explanation: This patient has **severe symptomatic aortic stenosis**: a valve area <1 cm2 with a mean gradient >40 mm Hg, plus the classic triad of **exertional angina, dyspnea, and syncope**. Once symptoms develop, the mean survival without valve replacement falls to 2-3 years and sudden death risk rises sharply, so **aortic valve replacement is the only effective treatment** and should be offered promptly regardless of age. Because his left ventricular function is preserved and he has no symptoms at rest, he is a straightforward surgical candidate.

distractorExplanations.a: Increasing a vasodilator does nothing for a fixed mechanical obstruction and can precipitate collapse by dropping preload across a stenotic valve.
distractorExplanations.b: Stress testing is contraindicated in symptomatic severe aortic stenosis and adds nothing once severity is already established by resting echocardiography.
distractorExplanations.c: Surveillance echocardiography is appropriate only for asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis; symptoms change the decision from watching to replacing.
distractorExplanations.d: Balloon valvuloplasty provides only short-term gradient relief in calcified adult valves and is reserved as a bridge in patients too unstable for definitive valve replacement.

teachingPoint: Symptoms in severe aortic stenosis — angina, dyspnea, or syncope — are the trigger for valve replacement; watchful waiting is for asymptomatic disease only.
note: Severe symptomatic AS: valve replacement.

subtopic: Biliary Obstruction from Pancreatic Head Mass
vignette: A 64-year-old man presents to his primary care physician with a 3-week history of progressive yellowing of his skin and eyes, dark urine, and pale stools. He has lost 8 kg over the past 2 months without trying. He denies abdominal pain, fever, or chills. His medical history includes type 2 diabetes mellitus diagnosed 6 months ago and a 40-pack-year smoking history. His temperature is 36.8°C, blood pressure is 134/86 mmHg, pulse is 78/min, and respirations are 16/min. Examination shows marked scleral icterus and a nontender abdomen with a palpable, enlarged gallbladder in the right upper quadrant. Laboratory studies reveal a total bilirubin of 14.2 mg/dL, direct bilirubin of 11.5 mg/dL, AST of 56 U/L, ALT of 48 U/L, alkaline phosphatase of 520 U/L, and lipase of 60 U/L. Abdominal ultrasound demonstrates a markedly dilated common bile duct of 15 mm and a dilated gallbladder without gallstones or wall thickening.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?

options.a: Upper endoscopy with endoscopic ultrasound
options.b: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography with brushings for cytology
options.c: Hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid scan
options.d: Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with pancreatic protocol
options.e: Serum CA 19-9 and carcinoembryonic antigen levels

explanation: This patient has **painless obstructive jaundice** with weight loss, new-onset diabetes, a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier sign), and a dilated biliary tree without gallstones, strongly suggesting a **pancreatic head mass**. The next diagnostic step is a **contrast-enhanced CT scan with pancreatic protocol** to visualize the mass, establish a tissue diagnosis through radiographic characteristics, and assess for surgical resectability. While CA 19-9 can be elevated, it is not diagnostic or sufficient for staging. ERCP with brushings may provide tissue but is typically performed after CT staging if the diagnosis remains unclear or for biliary decompression.

distractorExplanations.a: Endoscopic ultrasound is useful for local staging and fine-needle aspiration of pancreatic lesions but is typically performed after initial CT staging to assess vascular invasion or confirm diagnosis.
distractorExplanations.b: ERCP with brushings can provide cytology but is invasive and typically reserved for therapeutic decompression or when CT fails to establish a diagnosis; CT staging is performed first.
distractorExplanations.c: A HIDA scan evaluates gallbladder function and biliary patency in acute cholecystitis or biliary leak; it has no role in evaluating a suspected pancreatic mass.
distractorExplanations.e: Tumor markers like CA 19-9 are neither sensitive nor specific enough for diagnosis; they can be elevated in benign biliary obstruction and are used adjunctively for monitoring known disease.

teachingPoint: Painless obstructive jaundice with a dilated gallbladder (Courvoisier sign) and weight loss suggests pancreatic head cancer. A contrast-enhanced CT scan with pancreatic protocol is the first-line diagnostic test to visualize the mass, assess local invasion, and determine surgical resectability.
note: Explanation says CT establishes a tissue diagnosis.

subtopic: Thalassemia trait versus iron deficiency
vignette: A 26-year-old woman from Greece is evaluated during a pre-employment health examination. She feels well and reports no fatigue, no heavy menstrual bleeding, and a diet that includes red meat several times weekly. She takes no medications. Her physical examination is unremarkable. A complete blood count ordered as part of the examination shows hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL, mean corpuscular volume 66 fL, red blood cell count 6.1 million/μL, and normal white blood cell and platelet counts. The peripheral smear shows microcytic cells with minimal variation in shape and no target cells. Ferritin is 85 ng/mL, serum iron is 95 μg/dL, and transferrin saturation is 30%.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?

options.a: Order hemoglobin electrophoresis
options.c: Perform upper and lower gastrointestinal endoscopy
options.d: Begin a 3-month trial of oral iron supplementation
options.e: Repeat the complete blood count in 6 months

explanation: This patient's iron studies are normal, so her **microcytosis is not iron deficiency**. The key clue is **disproportionate microcytosis**: a mean corpuscular volume of 66 fL with a hemoglobin of 11.9 g/dL is far more microcytosis than the degree of anemia explains, and the **elevated red blood cell count** is characteristic of thalassemia trait, in which the marrow compensates for small cells by producing more of them. Her Mediterranean ancestry and the **Mentzer index** (MCV divided by RBC count, less than 13) both point to **thalassemia trait**. **Hemoglobin electrophoresis** is the confirmatory study, showing an elevated hemoglobin A2 in beta-thalassemia trait. No iron should be given, since her stores are already normal.

distractorExplanations.b: Soluble transferrin receptor is elevated in iron deficiency, which her normal iron studies already exclude.
distractorExplanations.c: Endoscopic evaluation is indicated for iron deficiency anemia in men and postmenopausal women; this premenopausal woman has no iron deficiency at all.
distractorExplanations.d: Iron therapy would do nothing here because her ferritin and iron studies are normal, and it risks iron overload in a patient who does not need it.
distractorExplanations.e: Deferring evaluation leaves a heritable hemoglobinopathy, relevant to future pregnancy counseling, undiagnosed.

teachingPoint: Microcytosis out of proportion to anemia, an elevated RBC count, normal iron studies, and a Mentzer index under 13 point to thalassemia trait, confirmed by hemoglobin electrophoresis with elevated hemoglobin A2.
note: Thalassemia trait: hemoglobin electrophoresis.

subtopic: Acute upper GI bleeding — resuscitation and endoscopy timing
vignette: A 68-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after vomiting bright red blood and coffee-ground material at home, followed by a large black stool. He has a history of osteoarthritis, for which he takes ibuprofen 600 mg twice daily and low-dose aspirin 81 mg daily. He also takes metoprolol for hypertension. On arrival, he is pale and diaphoretic. Vital signs are blood pressure 84/52 mmHg, heart rate 128 bpm, respiratory rate 24, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. He is drowsy but arousable and answers questions appropriately. Abdominal examination reveals epigastric tenderness without guarding; rectal examination shows maroon-coloured stool. Two large-bore peripheral IV catheters are placed. Stat laboratory results are pending. The nurse asks what to do next.
leadIn: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate next step in this patient's management?

options.a: Administer IV omeprazole 80 mg bolus followed by 8 mg/hour infusion
options.b: Perform emergent upper endoscopy within 12 hours
options.c: Begin rapid isotonic crystalloid infusion and prepare for blood transfusion
options.d: Administer IV erythromycin 250 mg to improve endoscopic visualisation
options.e: Administer IV octreotide 50 mcg bolus followed by 50 mcg/hour infusion

explanation: This patient presents with **acute upper GI bleeding** (haematemesis and melena) in the setting of chronic NSAID and aspirin use, and he is in **haemorrhagic shock** (hypotension, tachycardia, altered mental status). The immediate priority in any unstable GI bleed is **volume resuscitation** with rapid isotonic crystalloid infusion and preparation for blood transfusion to restore tissue perfusion before any diagnostic or therapeutic intervention. Endoscopy within 12 hours, IV PPI infusion, and prokinetic agents all have roles in upper GI bleeding management, but they must follow initial resuscitation.

distractorExplanations.a: IV PPI infusion is part of upper GI bleeding management but is initiated after or alongside resuscitation, not before haemodynamic stability is achieved.
distractorExplanations.b: Emergent endoscopy within 12 hours is indicated for diagnosis and haemostasis but must follow initial stabilisation; performing endoscopy in an unstable, under-resuscitated patient increases procedural risk.
distractorExplanations.d: IV erythromycin improves gastric visualisation during endoscopy but is an adjunct given 30–90 minutes before the procedure, not the first intervention in a patient in haemorrhagic shock.
distractorExplanations.e: IV octreotide reduces splanchnic blood flow and is used when variceal bleeding is suspected, but this patient's NSAID use and epigastric tendibility favour a non-variceal source; regardless, resuscitation takes priority over any pharmacotherapy.

teachingPoint: In any patient presenting with acute GI bleeding and signs of **haemorrhagic shock** (hypotension, tachycardia, altered mental status), the first and most critical step is **volume resuscitation** with isotonic crystalloid and preparation for transfusion. All subsequent interventions — IV PPI infusion, octreotide for suspected variceal bleeding, erythromycin for endoscopic visualisation, and **urgent endoscopy within 12 hours** — must follow or accompany initial haemodynamic stabilisation, never precede it.
note: Unstable UGIB: resuscitation first.

subtopic: Ductal-dependent critical coarctation in the neonate
vignette: A male infant is born at 39 weeks' gestation by spontaneous vaginal delivery; birth weight is 3.3 kg and Apgar scores are 8 and 9. He is discharged home on day 2 of life feeding well. On day 4 he is brought to the emergency department with poor feeding, rapid breathing, and lethargy. Temperature is 36.4°C, pulse is 186/min, respirations are 72/min, and blood pressure is 62/38 mm Hg in the right arm. He is pale and mottled with weak peripheral pulses overall; femoral pulses are impalpable while brachial pulses remain palpable. There is no murmur. The liver edge is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin. Capillary refill is 5 seconds. Laboratory studies show pH 7.18, bicarbonate 12 mEq/L, and lactate 7.8 mmol/L. Chest radiograph shows cardiomegaly with pulmonary venous congestion. Blood cultures are drawn and empiric antibiotics are started.
leadIn: In addition to intravenous fluids and inotropic support, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.a: Indomethacin intravenous administration
options.c: Immediate surgical repair of the aortic arch
options.d: Milrinone intravenous infusion
options.e: Prostaglandin E1 continuous infusion

explanation: A newborn who is well for the first 2 days and then collapses into **shock with absent femoral pulses and severe metabolic acidosis** has a **ductal-dependent obstructive left-heart lesion**, most commonly **critical coarctation of the aorta**: the descending aorta is perfused through the ductus arteriosus, and spontaneous ductal closure on day 2 to 3 precipitates cardiovascular collapse. The murmur is absent because the lesion itself is silent in the newborn. The immediate priority is to **reopen and maintain the ductus arteriosus with a prostaglandin E1 infusion**, which restores lower-body perfusion and allows stabilization before definitive surgical repair.

distractorExplanations.a: Indomethacin closes the ductus arteriosus; in this infant the ductus is the only route supplying the descending aorta, so closing it would be fatal.
distractorExplanations.b: Prostacyclin is a pulmonary and systemic vasodilator used in persistent pulmonary hypertension; it does not reopen the ductus arteriosus and would worsen systemic hypotension.
distractorExplanations.c: Definitive surgical repair is required, but the infant must first be stabilized with prostaglandin E1 and metabolic resuscitation; taking an unstable, acidotic neonate directly to the operating room is not the next step.
distractorExplanations.d: Milrinone may lower afterload but does nothing for the anatomic obstruction or the ductal dependency that caused the collapse.

teachingPoint: A well newborn who collapses into shock at 2-3 days of life has ductal closure unmasking a ductal-dependent lesion; absent femoral pulses point to critical coarctation, and the immediate step is prostaglandin E1 to reopen the ductus.
note: Critical coarctation in a neonate: PGE1.

subtopic: Chagas myocarditis — histologic finding
vignette: A 52-year-old man from rural Brazil is evaluated for progressive dyspnea and leg swelling over the past year. He has had longstanding difficulty swallowing and chronic constipation. Examination shows jugular venous distention, bibasilar crackles, an S3 gallop, and pitting edema of both legs. Echocardiography shows a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 28% and a small apical aneurysm. Endomyocardial biopsy shows a lymphocytic infiltrate in the myocardium, and a peripheral smear and serology are pending. Colon imaging shows a markedly dilated sigmoid colon.
leadIn: Which of the following histologic findings is most likely to be present on examination of this patient's myocardial tissue?

options.a: Caseating granulomas with central necrosis
options.b: Multinucleated giant cells with eosinophilic necrosis
options.c: Amastigote-filled pseudocysts within cardiac myocytes
options.d: Fibrinous pericardial exudate with frond-like projections
options.e: Intranuclear viral inclusion bodies with myocyte necrosis

explanation: The combination of a **dilated cardiomyopathy with an apical aneurysm**, GI dysmotility (dysphagia and megacolon), and residence in **rural Latin America** identifies chronic **Chagas disease** caused by *Trypanosoma cruzi*. In infected myocardium, the parasite replicates intracellularly, producing **amastigote-filled pseudocysts within cardiac myocytes** surrounded by a lymphocytic infiltrate — the specific finding that distinguishes Chagas myocarditis from other causes of dilated cardiomyopathy.

distractorExplanations.a: Caseating granulomas suggest tuberculosis or fungal infection, neither of which explains the megacolon and apical aneurysm in this epidemiologic setting.
distractorExplanations.b: Multinucleated giant cells with eosinophilic necrosis characterize giant cell myocarditis, a rapidly progressive disease of younger patients without the GI features of this case.
distractorExplanations.d: A fibrinous pericardial exudate would indicate uremic or viral pericarditis and would not cause the dilated cardiomyopathy or megacolon described.
distractorExplanations.e: Viral inclusions with myocyte necrosis would suggest cytomegalovirus or adenovirus myocarditis, which is acute and lacks the chronic GI dysmotility and apical aneurysm.

teachingPoint: Chronic Chagas disease causes dilated cardiomyopathy with apical aneurysm plus megacolon/megaesophagus; cardiac histology shows amastigote-filled pseudocysts within myocytes.
note: Chagas: amastigotes in myocytes (board convention; scarce in chronic phase).

subtopic: Obstructive PFT pattern with bronchodilator reversibility
vignette: A 28-year-old man presents with a two-year history of episodic wheeze and chest tightness, most often triggered by his cat and by exercise. He has never smoked and works as a software developer. On examination he has scattered expiratory wheezes. Spirometry is performed: FEV1 is 62% of predicted, FVC is 88% of predicted, and the FEV1/FVC ratio is 0.68. Fifteen minutes after four puffs of albuterol, FEV1 increases to 79% of predicted. His chest radiograph is unremarkable.
leadIn: Which set of findings best characterizes this patient's baseline pulmonary physiology?

options.a: Obstructive pattern with increased total lung capacity and reduced DLCO
options.b: Restrictive pattern with reduced total lung capacity and reduced DLCO
options.c: Obstructive pattern with increased total lung capacity and normal DLCO
options.d: Restrictive pattern with reduced total lung capacity and normal DLCO
options.e: Normal spirometry with reduced DLCO and normal total lung capacity

explanation: The low **FEV1/FVC ratio** with a preserved FVC defines an **obstructive pattern**. In asthma, air trapping during exacerbations and chronic hyperinflation raise the **total lung capacity**, while the alveolar-capillary membrane remains intact, so the **DLCO is normal or even increased**. The 17% absolute improvement in FEV1 after albuterol confirms the reversibility that distinguishes asthma from most other obstructive diseases.

distractorExplanations.a: A reduced DLCO with obstruction and hyperinflation suggests emphysema, where alveolar destruction impairs gas transfer; this patient's young age, no smoking history, and reversibility point away from emphysema.
distractorExplanations.b: A restrictive pattern with reduced DLCO characterizes interstitial lung disease, where both lung volumes and gas transfer fall together; his FVC was preserved and the ratio was reduced.
distractorExplanations.d: A restrictive pattern with normal DLCO suggests chest wall disease or neuromuscular weakness, which would not produce wheezing or a post-bronchodilator response.
distractorExplanations.e: His baseline FEV1 was only 62% of predicted with a reduced ratio, so baseline spirometry is clearly abnormal.

teachingPoint: Asthma shows an obstructive pattern (low FEV1/FVC) with hyperinflation (increased TLC) and a normal or increased DLCO, plus reversibility after a bronchodilator.
note: Asthma: obstructive, raised TLC, normal DLCO.

subtopic: Ulnar nerve — deep motor branch in the hand
vignette: A 28-year-old woman sustained a laceration across the medial wrist from broken glass. On examination, the fourth and fifth digits are hyperextended at the metacarpophalangeal joints and flexed at the interphalangeal joints. Sensation is absent over the palmar and dorsal surfaces of the medial one and a half fingers.
